## Overview

The Abazins, also known as the Abaza or Abazinians, are an ethnic group of the Northwest Caucasus closely related to the Abkhaz and Circassian peoples. They live mainly in Turkey, Syria, Jordan, Egypt, Karachay-Cherkessia and Stavropol Krai in the North Caucasus region of Russia. The Tapanta branch historically lived between the Besleney and Kabardian princedoms on the upper Kuban. According to the 2010 Russian census, there were 43,341 Abazins in Russia. Their culture and traditions are similar to those of the Circassians, while their historical language belongs to the Northwest Caucasian language family.

## Foodways

Historically, the Abazin engaged in animal herding and some farming.

## Language & religion

The Abaza language is a Northwest Caucasian language most closely related to Abkhaz and more distantly related to the Ubykh and Circassian languages. Two Abaza dialects are spoken in Karachay-Cherkessia: Ashkharua and Tapanta. The Abazins are dominantly Sunni Muslims. They first encountered Islam during migrations to the Abazinia region through contact with the Nogais and other Muslim people, and adopted Islam through the influence of Muslim merchants and missionaries from the 16th to 19th centuries.

commons_photos.title: Tombeau au pont de pierre sur le Couban by Giuseppe Bernardazzi (1829) - Version 2.jpg
commons_photos.description:
A historical drawing of a now-destroyed nine-sided Muslim mausoleum near the Stone Bridge (Каменный Мост) on the right bank of the Kuban River, near modern Karachayevsk. The tomb belonged to the Abazin Prince Ahmed-bek from the Kyachev family of the Tapanta tribe. It was drawn on October 16, 1829, by Giuseppe Bernardazzi during General Emanuel's expedition. This file is a digitally enhanced version of the original drawing.
In Leonid Lavrov's study, this monument is cataloged under number 509 (509. Гор. Карачаевск. Над окошком девятигранного мавзолея, который теперь не существует). The structure is depicted as a stone tomb with a pointed dome and an Ottoman Turkish inscription above the window.
The original inscription, organized line by line, reads:

[1] زیارتدن همان بر دعادر
[2] بوکون بکا ایسه یارین سکادر صاحب
[3] المرحوم کاج اوغلی احمد بك روحینه فاتحه
[4] سنه
[5] ١١٦٣
The contemporary Russian translation reads:
«От посещающего [требуется] только одна молитва. Если сегодня [это случилось] со мной, то завтра [это случится] с тобой. Обладатель умерший Ахмад-бек сын Каджа. Душе его — Фатиху! Год 1163».
The English translation, incorporating the Russian brackets, reads: "From the visitor [is required] only one prayer. If today [this happened] with me, then tomorrow [this will happen] with you. The owner [is the] deceased Ahmed-bek, son of Kadzha. To his soul — [recite] Al-Fatiha! Year 1163" (1749–1750 AD).

The drawing features two original annotations. The French inscription reads: Tombeau au pont de pierre sur le Couban. The Russian archival note indicates: В 3-х верстах выше церкви на р. Кубани на прав. берегу Кубани. The document was acquired in 1829 by Peter von Köppen from Bernardazzi and analyzed by translator P. I. Volochkov.
